Each package had introduced breaking changes that resulted in errors, version conflicts, and even the inability to run the project. The breaking changes in ESLint were the most frustrating. Several rules were deprecated, and new rule configurations required major changes to the `.eslintrc` file. Additionally, the plugin `eslint-plugin-import` began requiring newer versions of ESLint that weren’t backward compatible with my original configuration. ```bash npm install eslint@latest eslint-plugin-import@latest ``` Nodemon also underwent significant updates. The move to Nodemon 3.x came with breaking changes in how the watcher worked and how it interacted with my build scripts. The config settings I was using to handle auto-reloading became obsolete, causing the server to crash when certain files changed. ```json \"dev\": \"nodemon --watch src --exec node server.js\" ``` These breaking changes led to a cascade of dependency issues, where some packages required older versions of Node.js, while others demanded the latest version. name: DevSpark v0.1.0: Agent-Agnostic, Multi-User, and Built for Teams
description: How canonical prompts, thin shims, and per-user personalization let teams share governance while celebrating individual workflow.
keywords: DevSpark, multi-user, agent-agnostic, team collaboration, AI development, personalization, canonical prompts, thin shims, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, constitution, governance
subtitle: How canonical prompts, thin shims, and per-user personalization let teams share governance while celebrating individual workflow
author: Mark Hazleton
summary: DevSpark v0.1.0 introduces two reinforcing design pillars — agent-agnostic architecture and multi-user personalization — that solve a tension every team with AI coding agents faces: how to share standards without forcing uniformity. Canonical prompts live in one place, thin shims adapt them per platform, and /devspark.personalize lets each developer tailor commands without affecting anyone else. The result is a model where teams commit personalized prompts to git, making individual workflow choices visible, reviewable, and shareable.
conclusionSummary: The tension between consistency and individual productivity is real. Agent-agnostic architecture with multi-user personalization doesn't eliminate it — but it makes the trade-offs visible, reversible, and committed to version control where they belong.
conclusionKeyText: Pick one command — the one that annoys you most in its default form — and run /devspark.personalize on it. Live with the override for a week. Then look at what you changed and ask whether the team would benefit from it too. That's the loop.
conclusionText: v0.1.0 didn't set out to solve team collaboration from scratch. It set out to solve the specific problem that critics and peer reviewers kept surfacing: the framework assumed a single developer using a single agent. Real teams don't work that way. The fix wasn't a grand redesign — it was three reinforcing decisions: canonical prompts, thin shims, and personalized overrides committed to git. Sometimes the best architecture is the one that gets out of the way.

description: The new Centralized Agent Registry breaks down AI walled gardens — mix GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor on the same specs without the framework skipping a beat.

subtitle: The new Centralized Agent Registry lets your team mix GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor in the same repo — against the same specs, under the same constitution
author: Mark Hazleton
summary: DevSpark's latest release rebuilds the framework's core to be completely AI-agnostic. The new Centralized Agent Registry — a single agents-registry.json file — strips every hardcoded 'if Copilot do this, if Claude do that' decision out of the framework scripts and replaces it with dynamic configuration. Adding support for tomorrow's newest AI tool is now a one-line registry entry. More practically: the same Markdown spec that one developer refines with Copilot in VS Code can be picked up and implemented by a colleague using Claude Code in the terminal, then reviewed by a tech lead in Cursor — without the framework skipping a beat.
conclusionSummary: DevSpark's Centralized Agent Registry doesn't pick winners in the AI tool market. It makes the question irrelevant — by ensuring that whatever tool your developers trust, the framework's governance travels with them.
conclusionKeyText: Check your current agents-registry.json. If your preferred AI tool isn't listed, add a three-line entry pointing to its shim location. That's the whole upgrade path.
conclusionText: The AI development tool market is moving fast — new agents, new IDE integrations, new capabilities every month. A framework that hardcodes its agent assumptions will need constant maintenance just to stay current. The Centralized Agent Registry inverts that problem: the framework stays stable, and each new agent requires only configuration, not code. The spec stays plain Markdown. The constitution stays non-negotiable. The governance stays consistent. What changes is the team's ability to bring their best tools to the work — and that, finally, is how it should be.

name: DevSpark Monorepo Support: Governing Multiple Apps in One Repository
description: Per-app governance, scoped workflows, and dependency-aware reviews — without fragmenting your repository.

subtitle: Per-app governance, scoped workflows, and dependency-aware reviews — without fragmenting your repository
author: Mark Hazleton
summary: Monorepos give teams atomic commits and unified history, but they introduce governance problems: mixed review rules, scope ambiguity, and AI agents that can't tell one app from another. DevSpark's multi-app support solves this with an explicit application registry, layered governance that can't weaken repo-wide rules, and dependency-aware scope analysis — all backward-compatible and opt-in.
conclusionTitle: The Governance Problem Is a Design Problem
conclusionSummary: Monorepo governance doesn't require separate tooling per application — it requires explicit scope, layered rules, and the discipline to make boundaries visible.
conclusionKeyText: If your monorepo has more than two deployable services, run /devspark.add-application for each one. The act of declaring scope forces conversations about ownership, criticality, and dependencies that most teams are deferring.
conclusionText: The monorepo governance problem isn't new, but the AI coding agent dimension is. When your assistant treats six applications as one undifferentiated codebase, you get plans and reviews that conflate unrelated concerns. Making application boundaries explicit in a machine-readable registry is the smallest change that produces the largest improvement in AI-assisted monorepo development.
